brief.subject: Fake law firm debt collectors halted by FTC court order
brief.headline: Court Freezes Phantom Debt Collectors Posing as Lawyers, FTC Says
brief.dek: A court froze an alleged phantom debt operation, a landlord pays $49.75 million, and a car dealer settles over misleading advertised prices.
brief.lede: At the FTC's request, a federal court froze the assets of a debt collection operation accused of pressuring people to pay debts they often didn't owe.

sections.heading: Phantom Debt Collectors Shut Down
bullets: A federal court temporarily halted the operation and froze its assets after an FTC request.
Collectors allegedly posed as a law firm or claimed ties to attorneys to scare people into paying.
Threats to contact your employer or family were part of the alleged pressure campaign.
Many targeted consumers frequently did not owe the debts at all, so legal-sounding threats alone prove nothing.

sections.heading: Rental Giant Pays $49.75 Million
bullets: Progress Residential and owner Pretium Partners will pay $49.75 million to settle FTC and state charges.
The FTC and four states say renters were misled by deceptive rental pricing practices.
It is the largest enforcement matter the FTC has brought against a landlord, a signal for renters checking advertised rates.
Progress Residential is described as the nation's largest property manager of single-family rental homes.

sections.heading: Car Dealer Settles Over Price Ads
bullets: Stream Auto Outlet, a Long Island, New York dealership group, reached a settlement with the FTC.
The FTC said advertised prices were far lower than what buyers ultimately had to pay.
For car shoppers, the gap between the ad price and the final bill is worth checking before signing.
